pandas is a powerful Python package mainly used for data manipulation and analysis. It is one of the most important tools in data science because real-world data is usually large, messy, and stored in tables. pandas helps organize and work with this data efficiently.
The course introduces pandas step by step:
Chapter 1 focuses on DataFrames
Chapter 2 covers aggregating and analyzing data
Chapter 3 teaches slicing and indexing
Chapter 4 discusses:
visualization
missing data
importing data into DataFrames

pandas is built on NumPy and Matplotlib
pandas is built on top of two important Python libraries:
NumPy — provides fast multidimensional arrays and numerical operations.
Matplotlib — provides data visualization and plotting features.
Because pandas uses these libraries internally, it becomes both powerful and flexible for handling datasets.

Why pandas is popular
pandas is widely used in the data science community because it simplifies working with datasets. Millions of Python users rely on it for tasks such as:
cleaning data
filtering information
performing calculations
analyzing trends
preparing data for machine learning
visualizing results
It has become one of the standard tools for data analysis in Python.

Rectangular or Tabular Data
Most datasets are stored in rectangular (tabular) form, similar to spreadsheets or database tables.
Example: a dataset about dogs.
Each row represents one observation (one dog).
Each column represents a variable or property:
name
breed
age
weight
color
This table-like structure is exactly what pandas is designed to handle.

DataFrames
The main object in pandas is the DataFrame.
A DataFrame is a table with:
rows = observations
columns = variables/features
Each column contains values of the same data type, but different columns may contain different types.
Example:
age → integers
weight → floats
name → strings
This flexibility makes DataFrames better than regular NumPy arrays for mixed datasets.

Exploring a DataFrame
When receiving a new dataset, the first step is usually to explore and understand it.
pandas provides several useful methods and attributes for this.

.head()
The .head() method displays the first few rows of a DataFrame.
dogs.head()
This is useful for quickly previewing the dataset structure and contents.
By default, it shows the first 5 rows.

.info()
The .info() method gives technical information about the DataFrame.
dogs.info()
It shows:
column names
data types
number of non-missing values
memory usage
This is especially useful for checking missing data and understanding the structure of the dataset.

.shape
The .shape attribute returns the dimensions of the DataFrame.
dogs.shape
Output example:
(7, 4)
Meaning:
7 rows
4 columns
Unlike methods, attributes do not use parentheses.

.describe()
The .describe() method generates summary statistics for numerical columns.
dogs.describe()
It usually includes:
count
mean
standard deviation
minimum value
quartiles
maximum value
This gives a quick statistical overview of numeric data.

Components of a DataFrame
A DataFrame has three important parts.

1. Data Values → .to_numpy()
You can convert the DataFrame values into a NumPy array.
dogs.to_numpy()
This returns a 2D NumPy array containing only the raw data values.

2. Column Labels → .columns
The .columns attribute contains the column names.
dogs.columns
Example output:
Index(['name', 'breed', 'age'])

3. Row Labels → .index
The .index attribute stores row labels.
dogs.index
These labels may be:
row numbers
custom names
dates
IDs
Important note: Row labels are accessed using .index, not .rows.

pandas Philosophy
Python generally follows the idea that there should be one obvious way to solve a problem. pandas is different.
In pandas:
there are often multiple ways to do the same task
users can choose whichever method they prefer
This makes pandas:
very flexible
extremely powerful
slightly harder to learn at first
A good way to think about pandas is like a Swiss Army knife: it provides many tools for handling data efficiently.

Key Takeaways
pandas is a Python library for data analysis and manipulation.
The main pandas structure is the DataFrame.
DataFrames store data in rows and columns.
pandas works especially well with tabular data.
Important exploration tools include:
.head()
.info()
.shape
.describe()
DataFrames also contain:
values
column labels
row labels
pandas is built on top of NumPy and Matplotlib.

t.ke06sr99nxz8.title: Sorting and Subsetting
t.ke06sr99nxz8.content:
Sorting and Subsetting in pandas
Sorting and subsetting are two of the most important skills when working with pandas DataFrames. These techniques help you quickly focus on the most useful or interesting parts of your dataset.
A DataFrame can contain thousands or even millions of rows, so instead of looking at everything at once, you usually:
sort the data to organize it better
subset the data to focus only on specific rows or columns

Sorting Data
Sorting changes the order of the rows in a DataFrame.
In pandas, this is done using the .sort_values() method.

Sorting by One Column
Suppose you have a dogs DataFrame and want to sort dogs by weight.
dogs.sort_values("weight_kg")
This sorts the rows from smallest weight to largest weight by default.
Result:
lightest dog appears first
heaviest dog appears last

Sorting in Descending Order
To reverse the order, use the ascending=False argument.
dogs.sort_values("weight_kg", ascending=False)
Now the heaviest dogs appear first.

Sorting by Multiple Columns
You can also sort using more than one column.
dogs.sort_values(["weight_kg", "height_cm"])
This means:
sort by weight first
if weights are equal, sort by height
This is useful when several rows share the same values in one column.

Different Sort Directions for Multiple Columns
You can control the direction for each column separately using a list in ascending.
dogs.sort_values(
   ["weight_kg", "height_cm"],
   ascending=[True, False]
)
Meaning:
weight → ascending
height → descending
So rows with equal weight are ordered from tallest to shortest.

Subsetting Columns
Subsetting means selecting only the data you need.
To select one column:
dogs["name"]
This returns a pandas Series containing only the name column.

Selecting Multiple Columns
To keep multiple columns, use double square brackets.
dogs[["name", "height_cm"]]
Why double brackets?
outer brackets → subset the DataFrame
inner brackets → create a list of column names
The result is a smaller DataFrame containing only those columns.

Subsetting Rows
Rows are usually filtered using conditions that produce True or False.

Filtering Numeric Data
Example: dogs taller than 50 cm.
dogs["height_cm"] > 50
This produces a Boolean Series:
True if condition matches
False otherwise
To actually filter the DataFrame:
dogs[dogs["height_cm"] > 50]
Only rows where the condition is True are returned.

Filtering Text Data
You can also filter categorical or text columns.
Example: get only Labradors.
dogs[dogs["breed"] == "Labrador"]
The double equals == checks equality.

Filtering Dates
Dates can also be compared.
Example: dogs born before 2015.
dogs[dogs["date_of_birth"] < "2015-01-01"]
Date format used:
YYYY-MM-DD
This is the international standard format.

Filtering with Multiple Conditions
Sometimes one condition is not enough.
Example:
dogs taller than 50 cm
AND weighing more than 20 kg
dogs[
   (dogs["height_cm"] > 50) &
   (dogs["weight_kg"] > 20)
]
Important:
use parentheses around each condition
use:
& for AND
| for OR
In pandas, you do not use normal Python and and or for Series comparisons.

Filtering with .isin()
If you want multiple possible values from a category, .isin() is easier.
Example: dogs that are black or brown.
dogs[dogs["color"].isin(["Black", "Brown"])]
.isin() checks whether each value exists inside the list provided.

Key Takeaways
Sorting:
.sort_values() sorts rows
ascending=False reverses order
multiple columns can be used for sorting
Subsetting Columns:
single brackets → one column
double brackets → multiple columns
Subsetting Rows:
use logical conditions
conditions return Boolean values
place conditions inside square brackets
Useful filtering techniques:
numeric filtering
text filtering
date filtering
multiple conditions using & and |
.isin() for multiple category values
These operations are essential because most real-world data analysis involves:
organizing data
filtering relevant information
narrowing large datasets into useful insights

t.agkgxcliakxl.title: New Columns
t.agkgxcliakxl.content:
New Columns in pandas
When working with pandas DataFrames, the data you receive is often not exactly in the format you need. Because of this, one of the most common tasks in pandas is creating new columns based on existing data.
This process can also be called:
transforming a DataFrame
mutating a DataFrame
feature engineering
Feature engineering is especially important in data science and machine learning because new variables can reveal better insights from the data.

Adding a New Column
Creating a new column is straightforward in pandas.
The general format is:
df["new_column"] = calculation
Left side → name of the new column
Right side → calculation or transformation

Example: Converting Height to Meters
Suppose the dogs DataFrame has a column called height_cm.
To create a new column for height in meters:
dogs["height_m"] = dogs["height_cm"] / 100
What happens here:
pandas takes every value in height_cm
divides it by 100
stores the result in a new column called height_m
The original DataFrame is updated automatically.

Creating Columns Using Multiple Existing Columns
New columns can also be created using calculations involving several columns.

Example: Doggy BMI
BMI (Body Mass Index) is calculated as:
BMI = weight / (height²)
For dogs:
dogs["bmi"] = dogs["weight_kg"] / dogs["height_m"] ** 2
Explanation:
dogs["height_m"] ** 2 → squares the height values
weight is divided by squared height
results are stored in a new bmi column
This demonstrates how pandas performs calculations element-by-element across entire columns.

Combining Multiple pandas Operations
The real strength of pandas comes from chaining operations together.
You can:
create new columns
filter rows
sort data
select specific columns
all in a logical workflow.

Example: Finding Tall Skinny Dogs
Suppose we define skinny dogs as dogs with BMI below 100.
First, filter the DataFrame:
skinny_dogs = dogs[dogs["bmi"] < 100]
Next, sort by height in descending order:
skinny_dogs = skinny_dogs.sort_values(
   "height_cm",
   ascending=False
)
Finally, select only the columns we want:
skinny_dogs[["name", "height_cm", "bmi"]]
This produces a cleaner DataFrame focused only on the relevant information.

Why New Columns Are Important
Creating derived columns allows you to:
calculate statistics
convert units
classify observations
prepare features for machine learning
simplify analysis
Instead of manually calculating values one at a time, pandas automatically performs operations across entire columns efficiently.

Key Takeaways
New columns are created using:
df["new_column"] = calculation
Calculations can use:
constants
one column
multiple columns
pandas performs operations element-wise across rows automatically.
Creating new columns is commonly called:
mutation
transformation
feature engineering
pandas becomes especially powerful when combining:
filtering
sorting
column selection
new column creation
These transformations are a core part of real-world data analysis workflows.

t.3ejmflolppnf.title: Summary Statistics
t.3ejmflolppnf.content:
Summary Statistics in pandas
In pandas, summary statistics are numerical values that help describe and summarize a dataset. Instead of manually checking every row, summary statistics give a quick overview of the data and help identify patterns, trends, or unusual values.
This chapter focuses on aggregating data, which means combining many values into meaningful summaries.

Summarizing Numerical Data
One of the most common summary statistics is the mean (average). The mean gives an idea of the “center” of the data.
To calculate the mean of a column:
dogs["weight_kg"].mean()
This computes the average weight of all dogs in the dataset.

Common Summary Statistics
pandas provides many built-in statistical methods.
Some important ones are:
Method
Description
.mean()
Average value
.median()
Middle value
.mode()
Most common value
.min()
Smallest value
.max()
Largest value
.var()
Variance
.std()
Standard deviation
.sum()
Total sum
.quantile()
Specific percentile
Example:
dogs["height_cm"].median()
This returns the median height.

Summarizing Dates
Summary statistics also work for date columns.
For example:
dogs["date_of_birth"].min()
This gives the oldest dog's birth date because earlier dates are smaller.
Similarly:
dogs["date_of_birth"].max()
returns the youngest dog's birth date.

The .agg() Method
The .agg() method (short for aggregate) allows you to compute custom or multiple summary statistics.
You can create your own function and apply it to a column.

Example: 30th Percentile
def pct30(column):
   return column.quantile(0.3)
This function returns the 30th percentile of a column.
Using .agg():
dogs["weight_kg"].agg(pct30)
This computes the 30th percentile of dog weights.

Using .agg() on Multiple Columns
You can apply the same aggregation to several columns at once.
dogs[["weight_kg", "height_cm"]].agg(pct30)
This calculates the 30th percentile for both weight and height.

Multiple Summary Statistics at Once
.agg() can also calculate several statistics simultaneously.
Example:
def pct40(column):
   return column.quantile(0.4)
Now apply both functions:
dogs["weight_kg"].agg([pct30, pct40])
This returns:
30th percentile
40th percentile
for the same column.
This is useful when comparing different summaries together.

Cumulative Statistics
Unlike normal summary statistics that return one value, cumulative statistics return a running total or running calculation across rows.

Cumulative Sum
The .cumsum() method computes a running total.
dogs["weight_kg"].cumsum()
How it works:
first row → first value
second row → first + second
third row → first + second + third
and so on
The last value equals the total sum of the column.

Other Cumulative Methods
pandas also provides other cumulative functions:
Method
Description
.cumsum()
Cumulative sum
.cummax()
Running maximum
.cummin()
Running minimum
.cumprod()
Running product
These methods return an entire Series instead of one summary number.

Walmart Dataset
The course introduces a Walmart dataset to practice aggregation and summary statistics.
The dataset includes:
weekly sales
store IDs
store types
department IDs
holiday information
temperature
fuel prices
unemployment rates
This type of dataset is ideal for:
calculating averages
comparing stores
analyzing trends
summarizing performance

Key Takeaways
Summary statistics help quickly understand datasets without examining every row.
Important pandas methods include:
.mean()
.median()
.min()
.max()
.std()
.quantile()
The .agg() method:
applies custom functions
works on one or multiple columns
can compute multiple statistics simultaneously
Cumulative methods like:
.cumsum()
.cummax()
.cummin()
return running calculations across rows.
These tools are essential in real-world data analysis because they help transform raw data into meaningful insights quickly and efficiently.

t.van30921kk8y.title: Counting
t.van30921kk8y.content:
Counting and Summarizing Categorical Data in pandas
In pandas, summary statistics are not only useful for numbers. Sometimes, you also need to summarize categorical data such as:
dog breeds
colors
store types
departments
categories
The most common way to summarize categorical variables is through counting.

The Problem of Double Counting
Imagine a dataset containing vet visits.
A dog may visit the vet multiple times, meaning the same dog can appear in several rows.
Example:
name
breed
Max
Labrador
Stella
Chihuahua
Max
Labrador
If we directly count breeds, the same dog could be counted multiple times, leading to inaccurate results.
To avoid this, we first remove duplicates.

Removing Duplicate Rows
The .drop_duplicates() method removes repeated rows.

Dropping Duplicates Based on One Column
Suppose we only want one row per dog name.
vet_visits.drop_duplicates(subset="name")
This keeps only the first occurrence of each dog name.
However, this can create problems if different dogs share the same name.
Example:
Max the Labrador
Max the Chow Chow
One of them would disappear.

Dropping Duplicates Using Multiple Columns
To better identify unique dogs, we can use both:
name
Breed
vet_visits.drop_duplicates(
   subset=["name", "breed"]
)
Now pandas only removes rows where both the name and breed are duplicates.
This preserves dogs that share the same name but are different breeds.

Counting Categories with .value_counts()
Once duplicates are removed, we can count occurrences of each category.
Example:
unique_dogs["breed"].value_counts()
This counts how many dogs belong to each breed.
Output example:
Labrador     4
Chihuahua    2
Poodle       1
By default, results are sorted from highest count to lowest count.

Sorting Counts
You can control sorting using the sort argument.
unique_dogs["breed"].value_counts(sort=True)
This keeps the largest counts at the top.

Calculating Proportions
Instead of raw counts, you may want percentages or proportions.
Use normalize=True.
unique_dogs["breed"].value_counts(
   normalize=True
)
Output example:
Labrador     0.25
Chihuahua    0.15
Meaning:
25% are Labradors
15% are Chihuahuas
These are proportions of the total dataset.

Why Counting is Important
Counting categorical data helps answer questions like:
Which category appears most often?
What percentage belongs to each group?
Which values are rare?
How is the data distributed?
This is extremely common in:
surveys
customer analysis
sales data
machine learning preprocessing

Key Takeaways
Categorical data is summarized mainly through counting.
.drop_duplicates() removes repeated rows.
subset= specifies which columns determine duplicates.
Multiple columns can be used for more accurate duplicate handling.
Counting methods:
.value_counts() → counts occurrences
normalize=True → converts counts into proportions
These tools are essential for understanding distributions in categorical datasets and avoiding misleading duplicate counts.

t.j44lmkaauma.title: Grouped summary statistics
t.j44lmkaauma.content:
Grouped Summary Statistics in pandas
Grouped summary statistics let you calculate statistics for different categories or groups inside your dataset instead of calculating everything for the whole DataFrame at once. This is useful because comparing groups often reveals patterns and insights that would otherwise stay hidden.
For example, instead of asking:
“What is the average weight of all dogs?”
you can ask:
“What is the average weight for each dog color?” “Which breed is tallest on average?” “Do male dogs weigh more than female dogs?”
This is where the groupby() method becomes extremely powerful.

Why Use groupby()?
Without groupby(), you would have to manually create subsets for every category and calculate statistics one by one. That quickly becomes repetitive and messy.
For example, you could filter all black dogs, compute their mean weight, then repeat for brown dogs, white dogs, and so on. But that creates duplicate code and increases the chance of mistakes.
groupby() automates this process.

Basic Grouped Summary
Suppose we have a DataFrame called dogs with columns like:
color
breed
weight_kg
height_cm
If we want the average weight for each dog color, we can do:
dogs.groupby("color")["weight_kg"].mean()
What happens here?
Step by step:
groupby("color")
Splits the dataset into groups based on dog color.
["weight_kg"]
Selects the weight column.
.mean()
Calculates the average weight for each group.
The result might look like:
black    26.5
brown    21.3
white    18.7
This means black dogs weigh 26.5 kg on average, brown dogs 21.3 kg, and so on.

Multiple Summary Statistics with .agg()
You are not limited to just one statistic. Using .agg() allows you to calculate several statistics at once.
Example:
dogs.groupby("color")["weight_kg"].agg([min, max, sum])
This calculates:
Minimum weight
Maximum weight
Total weight
for each dog color.
The result becomes a small summary table.

Grouping by Multiple Columns
You can also group by more than one category.
Example:
dogs.groupby(["color", "breed"])["weight_kg"].mean()
Now pandas groups dogs by:
color
breed
This creates more detailed summaries.
Instead of:
“Average weight of black dogs”
you now get:
“Average weight of black Labradors” “Average weight of brown Poodles”
and so on.
This is useful when one grouping category is not enough.

Multiple Groups + Multiple Statistics
You can combine everything together:
dogs.groupby(["color", "breed"])["weight_kg"].agg([min, max, mean])
This gives grouped statistics for every breed-color combination.
Very powerful for data analysis.

Key Idea Behind groupby()
The overall process is:
Split the data into groups
Apply a calculation
Combine the results
This is often called:
Split → Apply → Combine
and it is one of the core ideas in pandas.

Important Notes
groupby() does NOT change the original DataFrame
It only creates grouped results.

Common summary methods after grouping
Some commonly used methods are:
.mean()
.sum()
.min()
.max()
.count()
.median()
.std()
.var()

.agg() is flexible
You can pass:
a single function
multiple functions
even custom functions
Example:
dogs.groupby("color")["weight_kg"].agg([mean, median, max])

Simple Mental Model
Think of groupby() like organizing students into classroom groups before calculating grades.
Without grouping:
One average for the whole school.
With grouping:
One average per classroom.
That’s exactly what pandas is doing with your data.

Quick Summary
groupby() is used to calculate statistics separately for categories or groups in your dataset.
Main patterns:
df.groupby("column")["value"].mean()
df.groupby("column")["value"].agg([min, max, mean])
df.groupby(["col1", "col2"])["value"].mean()
It is one of the most important tools in pandas because real-world data analysis almost always involves comparing groups.

t.m8ff97bp12rd.title: Pivot Tables
t.m8ff97bp12rd.content:
Pivot Tables in pandas
Pivot tables are another powerful way to calculate grouped summary statistics in pandas. If you have ever used Excel or Google Sheets, you may already be familiar with pivot tables. In pandas, they work similarly, but with Python code.
A pivot table helps you summarize and organize data by grouping values together and applying calculations such as averages, sums, or counts.

Basic Idea of a Pivot Table
Suppose you have a DataFrame of dogs with columns like:
color
breed
weight_kg
If you want the average weight for each dog color, you can use a pivot table.
dogs.pivot_table(values="weight_kg", index="color")
Understanding the arguments
values → the column you want to summarize
index → the column you want to group by
By default, pivot_table() calculates the mean (average).
So this code means:
“Group dogs by color and calculate the average weight.”

Changing the Summary Statistic
Pivot tables use the mean by default, but you can change the calculation using aggfunc.
Example:
dogs.pivot_table(
   values="weight_kg",
   index="color",
   aggfunc="median"
)
This calculates the median weight instead of the mean.
You can use many functions such as:
"mean"
"median"
"sum"
"min"
"max"
"count"

Multiple Statistics at Once
You can calculate several statistics together by passing a list into aggfunc.
Example:
dogs.pivot_table(
   values="weight_kg",
   index="color",
   aggfunc=["mean", "median"]
)
This creates a table containing both:
average weight
median weight
for every dog color.

Grouping by Two Variables
Pivot tables become more powerful when you summarize data across two categories.
Example:
dogs.pivot_table(
   values="weight_kg",
   index="color",
   columns="breed"
)
What happens here?
Rows represent dog colors
Columns represent dog breeds
Values inside the table are average weights
This creates a matrix-like summary table.

Missing Values (NaN)
Sometimes certain combinations do not exist.
For example:
maybe there are no black Chihuahuas
maybe there are no gray Labradors
In these cases, pandas displays:
NaN
which means:
“No data available.”

Filling Missing Values
You can replace missing values using fill_value.
Example:
dogs.pivot_table(
   values="weight_kg",
   index="color",
   columns="breed",
   fill_value=0
)
Now all missing values become 0.
This makes the table cleaner and easier to read.

Adding Totals with margins=True
Pivot tables can also calculate overall summaries automatically.
Example:
dogs.pivot_table(
   values="weight_kg",
   index="color",
   columns="breed",
   fill_value=0,
   margins=True
)
This adds:
a final row
a final column
called "All".
These contain summary statistics for:
all rows
all columns
the entire dataset
So you can instantly see:
average weight per color
average weight per breed
overall average weight
all in one table.

Difference Between groupby() and pivot_table()
Both can calculate grouped statistics, but they are often used differently.
groupby()
Best for:
flexible analysis
transformations
chaining operations
pivot_table()
Best for:
spreadsheet-style summaries
clean table layouts
comparing categories visually
You can often solve the same problem with either one.

Mental Model
Think of a pivot table like creating a report table.
For example:
Color
Labrador
Poodle
Chihuahua
Black
30
12
NaN
Brown
28
10
5
Instead of reading raw rows one by one, pivot tables organize data into a compact summary.

Important Parameters to Remember
Core arguments
values → what to summarize
index → row groups
columns → column groups
aggfunc → summary calculation

Useful optional arguments
fill_value → replaces missing values
margins=True → adds totals/overall summaries

Quick Examples
Average weight by color
dogs.pivot_table(
   values="weight_kg",
   index="color"
)

Median weight by color
dogs.pivot_table(
   values="weight_kg",
   index="color",
   aggfunc="median"
)

Multiple statistics
dogs.pivot_table(
   values="weight_kg",
   index="color",
   aggfunc=["mean", "max"]
)

Two-variable pivot table
dogs.pivot_table(
   values="weight_kg",
   index="color",
   columns="breed"
)

Key Takeaway
Pivot tables are a compact and powerful way to summarize data in pandas. They allow you to:
group data
calculate statistics
compare categories
create spreadsheet-style summaries
all with very little code.

t.sa49vbakeagj.title: Explicit indexes
t.sa49vbakeagj.content:
Explicit Indexes in pandas
In pandas, a DataFrame is made up of three main parts:
the actual data
column labels
row labels (called the index)
You already know that:
df.columns
shows the column names, while:
df.index
shows the row labels.
By default, pandas automatically uses numbers like 0, 1, 2, 3... as row indexes, but you can replace these with more meaningful values. This is called setting an index.

Setting a Column as the Index
Suppose you have a DataFrame of dogs with a name column.
You can make the dog names become the row labels using:
dogs = dogs.set_index("name")
Now the name column is no longer part of the main table columns. Instead, it becomes the index.
This makes the DataFrame easier to read and sometimes easier to subset.
One visual clue is that index values are displayed on the far left side of the DataFrame.

Resetting the Index
If you want to bring the index back as a normal column again, use:
dogs = dogs.reset_index()
This restores the default numbered index and moves the old index back into the DataFrame as a regular column.

Dropping the Index Completely
You can also remove the index entirely using:
dogs = dogs.reset_index(drop=True)
Here:
drop=True means: “Do not keep the old index as a column.”
So the custom index disappears completely.

Why Use Indexes?
Indexes make certain types of subsetting much cleaner and easier.
Without indexes, filtering rows can look more complicated.
Example without index:
dogs[dogs["name"].isin(["Bella", "Stella"])]
This works, but it is somewhat long.

If the name column is set as the index:
dogs.loc[["Bella", "Stella"]]
This is much simpler and easier to read.
The .loc[] method works directly with index labels.

Index Values Do NOT Need to Be Unique
Unlike primary keys in databases, pandas indexes can contain duplicates.
Example:
dogs = dogs.set_index("breed")
If there are multiple Labradors, the index can contain "Labrador" more than once.
Then:
dogs.loc["Labrador"]
returns all Labrador rows.

Multi-Level Indexes (Hierarchical Indexes)
You can also use more than one column as the index.
Example:
dogs = dogs.set_index(["breed", "color"])
Now the DataFrame has two index levels:
outer index → breed
inner index → color
This is called:
a multi-level index
or a hierarchical index
Both terms mean the same thing.

Subsetting Multi-Level Indexes
Selecting outer-level indexes
Example:
dogs.loc[["Labrador", "Chihuahua"]]
This returns all Labradors and Chihuahuas.

Selecting inner-level combinations
For deeper filtering, use tuples.
Example:
dogs.loc[[("Labrador", "Brown")]]
This means:
Give rows where:
breed = Labrador
color = Brown
Every condition inside the tuple must match.

Sorting by Index
Besides sorting by column values using:
sort_values()
you can sort using index labels with:
dogs.sort_index()
This sorts from outer index to inner index.

Controlling Index Sorting
You can customize sorting behavior using:
level
ascending
Example:
dogs.sort_index(level=["breed", "color"], ascending=[True, False])
This allows different sorting directions for different levels.

The Downsides of Indexes
Indexes are powerful, but they are somewhat controversial in pandas.
Why?
Because indexes are still data, but they are stored differently from normal columns.
This creates some issues:
1. More complicated syntax
Working with indexes uses different syntax (loc) compared to normal columns.
That means more things to remember.

2. Violates “tidy data” principles
Tidy data says:
every row = one observation
every column = one variable
Indexes are data that are not stored in columns, which breaks this structure somewhat.

3. Can increase bugs
Since pandas has:
column-based syntax
index-based syntax
you may accidentally mix them up.

Important Perspective
You do NOT always need indexes.
Many pandas users prefer keeping everything as normal columns because it is simpler and easier to debug.
However, indexes are still important because:
many pandas operations rely on them
many real-world datasets use them
you will often encounter them in other people's code
So understanding indexes is essential.

Mental Model
Think of indexes as labels for rows.
Normally rows are labeled:
0, 1, 2, 3
But you can replace them with meaningful identifiers like:
Bella, Max, Charlie
or even combinations like:
(Labrador, Brown)
This helps organize and access data more efficiently.

Quick Summary
Setting an index
df.set_index("column")

Resetting the index
df.reset_index()

Dropping the old index
df.reset_index(drop=True)

Selecting with .loc
df.loc["Bella"]

Multi-level index
df.set_index(["breed", "color"])

Sorting indexes
df.sort_index()

Key Takeaway
Indexes in pandas are special row labels that make certain operations, especially subsetting, cleaner and more powerful. They can simplify data access, support hierarchical organization, and improve readability, but they also introduce additional complexity.

t.g0h7wjiwhfrk.title: Slicing and subsetting with .loc and .iloc
t.g0h7wjiwhfrk.content:
Slicing and Subsetting with .loc and .iloc
Slicing is a way of selecting consecutive parts of a sequence or dataset. In Python, you first learn slicing with lists, then apply the same idea to pandas DataFrames. Understanding slicing is important because it allows you to quickly extract only the rows or columns you need from large datasets.
With Python lists, slicing uses positions (indexes). Remember that Python starts counting at 0. For example:
breeds[2:5]
This means:
start at position 2
stop before position 5
So elements at positions 2, 3, and 4 are included. The last position is not included in normal Python slicing.
You can also simplify slices:
breeds[:3]
This means “from the start up to position 3.”
And:
breeds[:]
means “take everything.”

Slicing DataFrames with .loc
For pandas DataFrames, slicing is usually done using .loc or .iloc.
Before slicing rows using index labels, it is important to sort the index first:
dogs = dogs.sort_index()
This prevents unexpected results.

.loc Uses Labels (Names)
.loc slices using row or column labels instead of numeric positions.
Example:
dogs.loc["Chow Chow":"Poodle"]
This selects all rows from "Chow Chow" to "Poodle".
A very important difference from normal Python slicing:
with .loc, the ending value IS included
So "Poodle" will appear in the result.

Multi-Level Index Slicing
When using hierarchical or multi-level indexes, slicing becomes more advanced.
Suppose the index has two levels:
breed
color
Trying to slice inner levels directly may fail:
dogs.loc["Tan":"Grey"]
This can return incorrect or empty results.
The correct way is to use tuples:
dogs.loc[
   ("Labrador", "Brown"):
   ("Schnauzer", "Grey")
]
Each tuple represents a complete index position.

Slicing Columns
Because DataFrames are two-dimensional, you can slice columns too.
Syntax:
dogs.loc[:, "name":"height_cm"]
The colon : means:
keep all rows
Then the second argument slices the columns.
This selects all rows, but only columns from "name" to "height_cm".

Slicing Rows and Columns Together
You can slice both dimensions at the same time:
dogs.loc[
   "Labrador":"Poodle",
   "name":"height_cm"
]
This filters:
specific rows
specific columns
all in one command.

Date Slicing
Dates are extremely common in pandas datasets.
If a date column becomes the index:
dogs = dogs.set_index("date_of_birth").sort_index()
you can slice using date strings.
Example:
dogs.loc["2014":"2016"]
This includes all rows between 2014 and 2016.
One useful pandas feature is partial date slicing. You do not always need full dates like "2014-01-01".
You can simply write:
dogs.loc["2015"]
and pandas understands you mean the entire year.

.iloc Uses Numeric Positions
While .loc uses labels, .iloc uses integer positions.
Example:
dogs.iloc[2:5, 1:4]
This means:
rows 2 to 4
columns 1 to 3
Important difference:
.iloc follows normal Python slicing rules
the ending position is NOT included
So position 5 and 4 are excluded.

Difference Between .loc and .iloc
A good way to remember them:
.loc → labels/names
.iloc → integer positions
Example:
dogs.loc["Bella":"Stella"]
uses names.
dogs.iloc[0:3]
uses row numbers.

Key Things to Remember
.loc
Uses labels/index names
Ending value is included
Good for readable filtering
.iloc
Uses numeric positions
Ending value is excluded
Similar to normal Python slicing
Slicing Tips
Always sort indexes before slicing
Use tuples for multi-level indexes
Use : to mean “everything”
Date slicing works very naturally in pandas

Example Summary
# Slice rows by labels
dogs.loc["A":"C"]

# Slice rows and columns
dogs.loc["A":"C", "name":"height_cm"]

# Slice by positions
dogs.iloc[0:3, 1:4]

# Slice dates
dogs.loc["2014":"2016"]
These slicing techniques are some of the most powerful tools in pandas because they allow you to quickly focus on the exact part of a dataset you want to analyze.

t.522kzxe41qyi.title: Working with pivot tables
t.522kzxe41qyi.content:
Working with Pivot Tables
Pivot tables are one of the most powerful tools in pandas for summarizing and analyzing grouped data. Earlier, you learned how to create them using pivot_table(). In this lesson, the focus is on how to work with pivot tables after they are created — especially how to subset them and compute additional statistics.
A pivot table in pandas is essentially just another DataFrame, but with grouped and summarized data. Because of this, all the DataFrame skills you already learned — especially .loc, slicing, and summary methods — can also be applied to pivot tables.

Creating a Pivot Table
A pivot table is created using .pivot_table().
Example:
dogs.pivot_table(
   values="height_cm",
   index="breed",
   columns="color"
)
This means:
values → the column to summarize
index → the groups shown as rows
columns → the groups shown as columns
By default, pandas calculates the mean.
So this pivot table shows:
the average height of each dog breed for each color.

Pivot Tables are DataFrames
A very important idea:
Pivot tables are just DataFrames with organized indexes.
Because of this, you can use everything you already know about DataFrames:
.loc[]
slicing
filtering
summary statistics
indexing
This makes pivot tables extremely flexible.

Using .loc[] with Pivot Tables
Since pivot tables have indexes, .loc[] works perfectly for selecting specific rows or columns.
Example:
pt.loc["Chihuahua":"Poodle"]
This slices breeds from "Chihuahua" to "Poodle".
You can also subset rows and columns together:
pt.loc[
   "Chihuahua":"Poodle",
   "Brown":"Gray"
]
This selects:
specific breeds (rows)
specific colors (columns)
at the same time.
This combination of .loc[] + slicing is one of the best ways to work with pivot tables.

Summary Statistics on Pivot Tables
Because pivot tables usually contain only numeric values, you can easily calculate statistics on them.
Example:
pt.mean()
This calculates the mean of each column.

Understanding the axis Argument
Many pandas methods use an axis argument.
The default is:
axis="index"
or equivalently:
axis=0
This means:
calculate statistics down the rows (vertically)
For a pivot table, this calculates a result for each column.

Calculating Across Rows
Example:
pt.mean(axis="index")
This computes the average for each color across all breeds.
So the calculation moves vertically down each column.

Calculating Across Columns
If you want calculations horizontally across columns, use:
pt.mean(axis="columns")
This computes the average for each breed across all colors.
So now the calculation moves horizontally across each row.

Why axis Matters More for Pivot Tables
In normal DataFrames, columns often contain different data types:
text
dates
numbers
Because of that, calculations across columns often do not make sense.
But pivot tables are special because:
almost every value is numeric
every column usually represents the same type of measurement
That is why operations like .mean(axis="columns") become very useful with pivot tables.

Quick Comparison
axis="index" (default)
Calculates vertically
Produces one result per column
Example:
pt.mean(axis="index")

axis="columns"
Calculates horizontally
Produces one result per row
Example:
pt.mean(axis="columns")

Example Workflow
# Create pivot table
pt = dogs.pivot_table(
   values="height_cm",
   index="breed",
   columns="color"
)

# Subset breeds
pt.loc["Chihuahua":"Poodle"]

# Mean for each color
pt.mean()

# Mean for each breed
pt.mean(axis="columns")

Key Takeaways
Pivot tables are powerful because they combine:
grouping
aggregation
reshaping
into a single structure.
Once created, you can treat them like normal DataFrames and use:
.loc[]
slicing
.mean()
.sum()
.max()
.min()
and many other pandas operations on them.
The axis argument is especially important because it controls the direction of calculations:
axis="index" → down columns
axis="columns" → across rows

t.8kt82i7ghmlo.title: Visualizing your data
t.8kt82i7ghmlo.content:
Visualizing Your Data
Data visualization is one of the most important parts of data analysis because it helps transform raw numbers into something easier to understand. Instead of only reading tables of values, plots allow you to quickly notice patterns, trends, relationships, and outliers in your data.
In pandas, plotting is closely connected with the matplotlib library. Before creating visualizations, you usually import:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
Just like pd is the common alias for pandas, plt is the standard alias for matplotlib.pyplot.
After creating a plot, you often need:
plt.show()
to actually display it.

Histograms
A histogram is used to visualize the distribution of a numeric variable. It groups values into ranges called bins and shows how many observations fall into each range.
Example:
dog_pack["height_cm"].hist()
plt.show()
This creates a histogram of dog heights.
The:
x-axis represents the height ranges
y-axis represents how many dogs fall into each range
Histograms are useful for understanding:
where most values are concentrated
whether data is spread out
whether the distribution is symmetric or skewed

Changing the Number of Bins
You can control how detailed the histogram is using the bins argument.
Example:
dog_pack["height_cm"].hist(bins=20)
plt.show()
fewer bins → simpler overview
more bins → more detailed distribution
Choosing the right number of bins helps make patterns clearer.

Bar Plots
Bar plots are useful for comparing categories.
For example, if you want to compare the average weight of each dog breed:
avg_weight = dog_pack.groupby("breed")["weight_kg"].mean()
Then create a bar plot:
avg_weight.plot(kind="bar")
plt.show()
Each bar represents a breed, and the height of the bar represents the average weight.

Adding a Title
Plots become easier to understand when labeled properly.
Example:
avg_weight.plot(
   kind="bar",
   title="Average Weight per Breed"
)
plt.show()
Titles help explain what the visualization is showing.

Line Plots
Line plots are excellent for showing how data changes over time.
Example:
sully.plot(
   x="date",
   y="weight_kg",
   kind="line"
)
plt.show()
This visualizes Sully’s weight over time.
Line plots are commonly used for:
time series data
trends
growth or decline
tracking changes

Rotating Axis Labels
Sometimes date labels overlap and become hard to read.
You can rotate labels using:
sully.plot(
   x="date",
   y="weight_kg",
   kind="line",
   rot=45
)
plt.show()
rot=45 rotates labels by 45 degrees.

Scatter Plots
Scatter plots are used to examine relationships between two numeric variables.
Example:
dog_pack.plot(
   x="height_cm",
   y="weight_kg",
   kind="scatter"
)
plt.show()
Each point represents one dog.
This helps identify:
correlations
trends
clusters
outliers
In this example, taller dogs generally weigh more.

Layering Plots
You can place multiple plots on top of each other to compare groups.
Example:
dog_pack[dog_pack["sex"] == "F"]["height_cm"].hist()
dog_pack[dog_pack["sex"] == "M"]["height_cm"].hist()
plt.show()
This overlays histograms for female and male dogs.

Adding a Legend
When multiple plots overlap, it may be unclear which is which.
Use:
plt.legend(["Female", "Male"])
to label the plots.
Example:
plt.legend(["Female", "Male"])
plt.show()

Transparency with alpha
Overlapping plots can block each other visually. The alpha argument controls transparency.
Values:
0 → fully transparent
1 → fully opaque
Example:
dog_pack[dog_pack["sex"] == "F"]["height_cm"].hist(alpha=0.5)

dog_pack[dog_pack["sex"] == "M"]["height_cm"].hist(alpha=0.5)

plt.legend(["Female", "Male"])
plt.show()
This makes both histograms easier to compare.

Choosing the Right Plot
Different plots are useful for different situations:
Histogram → distribution of one numeric variable
Bar plot → compare categories
Line plot → trends over time
Scatter plot → relationship between two numeric variables

Example Summary
# Histogram
dog_pack["height_cm"].hist()

# Bar plot
avg_weight.plot(kind="bar")

# Line plot

t.oog1odoch7uf.title: Missing values
t.oog1odoch7uf.content:
Missing Values in pandas
In real-world datasets, missing values are extremely common. Data is rarely perfect — sometimes information is not recorded, sensors fail, users skip inputs, or files become incomplete. Because of this, knowing how to detect and handle missing values is an essential skill in data analysis.
In pandas, missing values are represented by:
NaN
which stands for:
“Not a Number”
Even though the name sounds numeric, NaN is used for many types of missing data in pandas.

Why Missing Values Matter
Missing data can affect:
calculations
averages
machine learning models
visualizations
filtering and grouping
For example, if some dog weights are missing because the scale was broken, calculations involving weight may become inaccurate or incomplete.
That’s why one of the first things you should do when receiving a new dataset is check for missing values.

Detecting Missing Values with .isna()
The .isna() method checks every value in a DataFrame and returns:
True → value is missing
False → value exists
Example:
dogs.isna()
This creates a DataFrame of Booleans.
Example result:
name
weight_kg
False
False
False
True
However, for large datasets, this output can be difficult to read.

Checking if Columns Contain Missing Values
To see whether a column contains any missing values, combine:
.isna().any()
Example:
dogs.isna().any()
Result:
name         False
weight_kg     True
height_cm    False
This means:
weight_kg contains at least one missing value
other columns do not

Counting Missing Values
Since True is treated as 1 in Python, summing Boolean values counts the number of missing entries.
Example:
dogs.isna().sum()
This returns the number of missing values per column.
Example output:
name         0
weight_kg    2
height_cm    0
So there are:
2 missing weights
no missing names or heights

Visualizing Missing Values
You can plot the number of missing values using a bar plot.
Example:
dogs.isna().sum().plot(kind="bar")
plt.show()
This helps quickly identify which columns have the most missing data.
Visualization becomes especially useful in large datasets with many variables.

Removing Missing Values with .dropna()
One approach is to remove rows that contain missing values.
Example:
dogs.dropna()
This removes all rows where at least one value is missing.

Important Consideration
Dropping rows is simple, but it can be risky.
If many rows contain missing data:
you may lose a large part of your dataset
your analysis may become biased
So use .dropna() carefully.

Replacing Missing Values with .fillna()
Instead of deleting rows, you can replace missing values.
Example:
dogs.fillna(0)
This replaces all NaN values with 0.

Filling with Other Values
You can also fill missing values using:
averages
medians
text labels
calculated values
Example:
dogs["weight_kg"].fillna(
   dogs["weight_kg"].mean()
)
This replaces missing weights with the average weight.
This is often better than removing data entirely.

Common Missing Value Workflow
A typical workflow looks like this:
1. Detect missing values
dogs.isna()
2. Count them
dogs.isna().sum()
3. Decide what to do
remove rows → .dropna()
replace values → .fillna()

Example Summary
# Detect missing values
dogs.isna()

# Check columns with missing data
dogs.isna().any()

# Count missing values
dogs.isna().sum()

# Remove rows with missing values
dogs.dropna()

# Replace missing values
dogs.fillna(0)

Key Takeaways
Missing values are a normal part of data analysis, and pandas provides powerful tools to handle them.
Important methods include:
.isna() → detect missing values
.any() → check if missing values exist
.sum() → count missing values
.dropna() → remove missing data
.fillna() → replace missing data
The best method depends on the situation:
small amount of missing data → dropping may be fine
large amount of missing data → filling is often better
Handling missing values properly helps ensure your analysis remains accurate and reliable.

t.9q0hm73ouxqh.title: Creating DataFrames
t.9q0hm73ouxqh.content:
Creating DataFrames in pandas
After learning how to manipulate and analyze DataFrames, the next important skill is learning how to create them. In pandas, a DataFrame is the main structure used to store tabular or rectangular data, similar to a spreadsheet or SQL table.
Before creating DataFrames, it’s important to understand dictionaries, because pandas heavily uses them when building DataFrames.
A dictionary in Python stores data as key-value pairs. The key acts like a label, while the value is the actual data connected to that label.
Example:
book = {
   "title": "Charlotte's Web",
   "author": "E.B. White"
}
Here:
"title" and "author" are keys
"Charlotte's Web" and "E.B. White" are values
You can access values using square brackets:
book["title"]
This returns:
Charlotte's Web

Two Main Ways to Create DataFrames
There are many ways to create DataFrames, but this lesson focuses on two common methods:
List of dictionaries → build DataFrame row by row
Dictionary of lists → build DataFrame column by column

1. Creating a DataFrame from a List of Dictionaries (Row-Based)
In this method, each dictionary represents one row of data.
You first create a list, then place dictionaries inside it.
Example:
import pandas as pd

list_of_dicts = [
   {
       "name": "Ginger",
       "breed": "Dachshund",
       "height_cm": 22,
       "weight_kg": 10
   },
   {
       "name": "Scout",
       "breed": "Dalmatian",
       "height_cm": 59,
       "weight_kg": 25
   }
]

dogs = pd.DataFrame(list_of_dicts)

print(dogs)
Output:
    name       breed  height_cm  weight_kg
0  Ginger   Dachshund         22         10
1   Scout  Dalmatian         59         25
How it works
Each dictionary becomes:
one row in the DataFrame
Each key becomes:
a column name
Each value becomes:
the data inside that row and column
This approach is useful when your data naturally comes row-by-row, such as:
API responses
JSON objects
manually entered records

2. Creating a DataFrame from a Dictionary of Lists (Column-Based)
In this method, each key is a column name, and each value is a list containing all values for that column.
Example:
import pandas as pd

dict_of_lists = {
   "name": ["Ginger", "Scout"],
   "breed": ["Dachshund", "Dalmatian"],
   "height_cm": [22, 59],
   "weight_kg": [10, 25]
}

dogs = pd.DataFrame(dict_of_lists)

print(dogs)
Output:
    name       breed  height_cm  weight_kg
0  Ginger   Dachshund         22         10
1   Scout  Dalmatian         59         25
How it works
Keys become column names
Lists become column values
Each list must usually have the same length
This method is often cleaner and easier when working with structured data.

Comparing the Two Methods
List of Dictionaries
Built row by row
Good for record-style data
Flexible for irregular data
Example mindset:
“Here is one dog's information.”

Dictionary of Lists
Built column by column
Cleaner for organized datasets
Common in data analysis
Example mindset:
“Here are all the dog names, all the breeds, all the heights…”

Big Picture
A pandas DataFrame is basically:
rows = observations/items
columns = variables/features
These creation methods simply provide different ways to organize the same data before converting it into a DataFrame.
You can think of it like this:
Method
Think About
List of dictionaries
Rows
Dictionary of lists
Columns

Important pandas Function
The key function used is:
pd.DataFrame()
This converts Python data structures into a DataFrame.

Key Takeaways
DataFrames store tabular data in pandas.
Dictionaries use key-value pairs.
You can create DataFrames:
row-by-row using a list of dictionaries
column-by-column using a dictionary of lists
pd.DataFrame() converts Python structures into DataFrames.
Column names usually come from dictionary keys.

t.3nn0988lkfrg.title: Reading and writing CSVs
t.3nn0988lkfrg.content:
Reading and Writing CSV Files in pandas
So far, you've learned how to manually create DataFrames, but in real-world data analysis, datasets are usually already stored in files. One of the most common file formats used for storing tabular data is the CSV file.
CSV stands for Comma-Separated Values. It is a simple text file format where:
each row of data is placed on a new line
each value is separated by commas
Because CSV files are simple and universal, almost every programming language, spreadsheet software, and database system can read and write them. This makes CSV one of the most widely used formats for sharing data.

What a CSV File Looks Like
Example CSV file:
name,breed,height_cm,weight_kg
Ginger,Dachshund,22,10
Scout,Dalmatian,59,25
This is basically the same structure as a DataFrame:
columns at the top
rows underneath

Reading a CSV File into pandas
To load a CSV file into a pandas DataFrame, pandas provides the function:
pd.read_csv()
Example:
import pandas as pd

dogs = pd.read_csv("new_dogs.csv")

print(dogs)
What happens here?
pd.read_csv() reads the CSV file
pandas converts the file into a DataFrame automatically
the variable dogs now stores the DataFrame
This is much faster and more practical than manually typing data into Python.

Manipulating the DataFrame
Once the CSV is loaded into a DataFrame, you can use all the pandas operations you've learned.
For example, creating a BMI column:
dogs["height_m"] = dogs["height_cm"] / 100

dogs["bmi"] = dogs["weight_kg"] / dogs["height_m"] ** 2
This adds new columns directly into the DataFrame.

Writing a DataFrame Back to CSV
After modifying the DataFrame, you may want to save the updated data.
You can convert a DataFrame back into a CSV file using:
DataFrame.to_csv()
Example:
dogs.to_csv("new_dogs_with_bmi.csv")
What this does
takes the DataFrame
converts it into CSV format
saves it as a new file
The new CSV file now contains the updated BMI column.

Complete Example
import pandas as pd

# Read CSV file
dogs = pd.read_csv("new_dogs.csv")

# Create height in meters
dogs["height_m"] = dogs["height_cm"] / 100

# Create BMI column
dogs["bmi"] = dogs["weight_kg"] / dogs["height_m"] ** 2

# Save updated DataFrame
dogs.to_csv("new_dogs_with_bmi.csv")

Important pandas Functions
Reading CSV files
pd.read_csv("file_name.csv")
Used to:
load CSV data into a DataFrame

Writing CSV files
DataFrame.to_csv("file_name.csv")
Used to:
save DataFrames as CSV files

Big Picture
The usual pandas workflow is:
Read data from a file
Store it in a DataFrame
Analyze or manipulate the data
Save the updated data
Example workflow:
CSV File → pandas DataFrame → Data Analysis → Updated CSV File
This is one of the core workflows in data science and data analysis.

Key Takeaways
CSV files store tabular data using commas.
pd.read_csv() loads CSV files into pandas DataFrames.
Once loaded, DataFrames can be analyzed and modified.
to_csv() saves DataFrames back into CSV files.
CSV is widely used because it is simple and compatible with many tools.

Inner Join in pandas
In real-world data analysis, information is often split across multiple tables or DataFrames. Instead of storing everything in one huge table, datasets are usually organized separately based on topic. Because of this, an important skill in pandas is learning how to combine tables together.
In pandas, combining tables is commonly called:
merging
or sometimes joining
In this course, both terms mean essentially the same thing.

Big Picture of Merging
Imagine you have two tables:
Table 1 — Ward Government Data
ward

address

Person A
Address A

Person B
Address B

Table 2 — Census Data
ward
population

Both tables contain a common column:
ward
This shared column allows pandas to connect related rows together.

What is an Inner Join?
An inner join returns only the rows where matching values exist in BOTH tables.
Think of it like:
“Keep only the rows that successfully match.”
If ward 2 exists in both tables:
they get combined
If a ward exists in only one table:
it gets excluded

Using merge()
The main pandas function used for joining tables is:
merge()
Basic syntax:
merged_df = left_table.merge(right_table, on="common_column")
Example:
wards_census = wards.merge(census, on="ward")
What this means
Start with wards
Merge with census
Match rows using the ward column

How merge() Works
Suppose:
wards table

no matching ward data

Important merge() Arguments
on=
Specifies the column used to match rows.
Example:
on="ward"

Column Order in Result
The table written first becomes the “left” table.
Example:
wards.merge(census, on="ward")
Result:
columns from wards
then columns from census

Overlapping Column Names
Sometimes both tables contain columns with the same name.
Example:
address
zip
pandas automatically avoids duplicate names by adding suffixes:
address_x
address_y
Where:
_x → left table
_y → right table

Using Custom Suffixes
You can make suffixes more readable using:
suffixes=
Example:
wards.merge(
   census,
   on="ward",
   suffixes=("_ward", "_cen")
)
Result:
address_ward
address_cen
This makes it easier to understand which table each column came from.

General Structure of an Inner Join
merged_df = left_df.merge(
   right_df,
   on="column_name"
)
With suffixes:
merged_df = left_df.merge(
   right_df,
   on="column_name",
   suffixes=("_left", "_right")
)

Big Concept to Remember
Merging is basically:
matching related rows from different tables using a common column.
The common column is often called:
key
join key
merge key
Examples:
id
customer_id
ward
employee_number

Why Merging is Important
Real datasets are usually separated into multiple tables because:
data is cleaner
easier to maintain
avoids repetition
For example:
customer info in one table
orders in another
payments in another
Merging allows you to combine them for analysis.
This is one of the most important skills in:
pandas

data science

Key Takeaways
merge() combines DataFrames together.

on= specifies the matching column.

t.mtby4njtaxhy.title: One-to-Many Relationships
t.mtby4njtaxhy.content:
One-to-Many Relationships in pandas
In the previous lesson, you learned how to merge two DataFrames using the merge() method. In this lesson, the focus is on understanding relationships between tables, especially the one-to-many relationship.
Before learning one-to-many, it helps to quickly review one-to-one relationships.
A one-to-one relationship means that each row in one table matches exactly one row in another table. For example, the wards table and the census table both contain one row per ward. Ward 3 in the first table matches only ward 3 in the second table. Since there is only one population record for each ward, the relationship is naturally one-to-one.
Example idea:
One ward → one census record
One row in the left table → one row in the right table

A one-to-many relationship is different. In this case, one row in the left table can match multiple rows in the right table.
The example used is the relationship between:
the wards table
the licenses table
The wards table contains information about each ward, while the licenses table contains many business licenses. Since many businesses can exist inside one ward, a single ward can appear multiple times in the licenses table.
So the relationship becomes:
One ward → many businesses

Both tables are connected using the ward column.
When using:
wards.merge(licenses, on="ward")
pandas automatically handles the one-to-many relationship.
If ward 1 has many businesses, the row for ward 1 from the wards table will be repeated for every matching business in the licenses table.
This is important because it explains why merged tables can suddenly become much larger.
For example:
Original wards table: 50 rows
After merging with licenses: 10,000 rows
The number of rows increases because each ward may match many business records.

Key Idea
In a one-to-many relationship:
The left table usually contains unique values.
The right table can contain repeated values for the matching column.
Merging repeats rows from the left table whenever multiple matches exist.

Important Notes
One-to-One Relationship
One row matches exactly one row.
Example: wards ↔ census
One-to-Many Relationship
One row matches several rows.
Example: wards ↔ licenses
pandas Behavior
The same merge() syntax is used.
pandas automatically duplicates matching rows when needed.
Row counts often increase after merging.

Example Structure
wards table

Notice how ward 1 and Joe appear twice because there are two businesses in ward 1.

Main Takeaway
A one-to-many merge is extremely common in real-world datasets. One category, customer, location, or ID often connects to many records in another table. pandas handles this automatically during merges, but you should always expect the resulting DataFrame to potentially have many more rows than the original table.

t.wj831piomyun.title: Merging Multiple DataFrames
t.wj831piomyun.content:
Merging Multiple DataFrames
In the previous lesson, you learned how to merge two tables together using merge(). In real-world data analysis, though, information is often spread across several different tables, not just two. Because of this, it’s very common to merge multiple DataFrames together step by step.
The lesson continues using datasets from the city of Chicago. Previously, there were two tables:
licenses → contains business license information
wards → contains information about Chicago wards and government offices
Now, a third table is introduced:
grants → contains information about businesses that received small business grant money
The goal is to combine all this information together so we can analyze things like:
which businesses received grants
where those businesses are located
which wards received the most grant money

Connecting Multiple Tables
To combine all the information, the process is done in stages.
First:
grants.merge(licenses, on=["address", "zip"])
Then:
merged_table.merge(wards, on="ward")
This creates one final DataFrame containing:
business information
grant information
ward information

Why Merge on Multiple Columns?
A very important concept introduced here is merging using more than one column.
At first glance, merging on only zip might seem enough, but it creates incorrect matches because many businesses can share the same zip code.
Similarly, merging only on address could also cause problems because addresses might repeat in different places.
The safer solution is to merge using BOTH:
address
zip
This ensures that a row only matches when BOTH values are the same.
Example:
grants.merge(licenses, on=["address", "zip"])
Notice that the on argument now receives a list instead of a single column name.

Key Idea About Multi-Column Merges
When merging on multiple columns:
on=["address", "zip"]
pandas requires ALL listed columns to match before rows are combined.
This helps avoid incorrect duplicates or mismatched data.

Chaining Multiple Merges
You can continue merging more tables one after another.
Example structure:
grants.merge(licenses, on=["address", "zip"]) \
     .merge(wards, on="ward")
The backslash \ is used for line continuation so Python treats it as one statement spread across multiple lines.
This technique keeps long merge operations cleaner and easier to read.

Result of Multiple Merges
After combining the tables, you now have a richer dataset containing:
grant amounts
business details
ward details
Once all the data is connected, you can perform analysis more easily.
For example:
calculate total grant money per ward
compare wards
visualize which wards received more funding
This is one of the biggest reasons merging is important in data analysis: it allows information from different sources to work together.

Important Concepts
Merging on Multiple Columns
Use a list inside on.
on=["address", "zip"]
Both columns must match.

Chaining Merges
You can merge several DataFrames in sequence.
df1.merge(df2).merge(df3)

Why This Matters
Real datasets are often separated across multiple tables.
You may need to combine:
customer data
transaction data
product data
location data
before meaningful analysis can happen.

Main Takeaway
Merging multiple DataFrames is a core skill in pandas because real-world data is rarely stored in one perfect table. pandas allows you to combine many datasets together step by step, and you can even merge using multiple matching columns to make the joins more accurate and reliable.

t.uoh31emdknho.title: Left Join in pandas
t.uoh31emdknho.content:
Left Join in pandas
In the earlier lessons, you learned how to merge tables using the merge() method. By default, pandas performs an inner join, which only keeps rows where matching values exist in both tables.
This lesson introduces another type of merge called the left join.
A left join keeps:
all rows from the left table
only the matching rows from the right table
If no match is found in the right table, pandas fills the missing values with NaN.

Quick Review of Inner Join
An inner join only returns rows where the key column exists in BOTH tables.
Example idea:
Left Table
Right Table
Result
Match exists
Match exists
Row kept
No match
—
Row removed
So unmatched rows disappear completely.

What Makes Left Join Different?
A left join preserves every row from the left table even if no match exists in the right table.
Example idea:
Left Table
Right Table
Result
Match exists
Match exists
Combined row
No match
—
Left row kept, right side becomes NaN
This is useful when the left table contains the main dataset you want to preserve.

Example Using Movies Dataset
The lesson uses data from The Movie Database.
There are two tables:
movies
Contains:
movie ID
title
popularity
This table has around 4,803 rows.

taglines
Contains:
movie ID
movie tagline
This table has fewer rows, meaning not every movie has a tagline.

Performing a Left Join
movies.merge(taglines, on="id", how="left")

Breaking Down the Code
movies
This is the left table.
All rows from this table will remain in the result.

taglines
This is the right table.
Only matching rows will be added.

on="id"
The id column is the key used to connect the tables.

how="left"
Specifies that the merge should be a left join.
Without this argument, pandas uses an inner join by default.

What Happens After the Merge?
If a movie has a matching tagline:
the tagline appears in the merged result
If a movie does NOT have a tagline:
the movie row is still kept
the tagline column becomes NaN
Example:
id
title
tagline
1
Movie A
"Epic adventure"
2
Movie B
NaN
Movie B stays because it came from the left table.

Important Observation About Row Counts
Since:
the left table (movies) has 4,803 rows
the relationship is one-to-one
the merged table keeps essentially the same number of rows.
That’s one important property of left joins:
In a one-to-one relationship, a left join usually returns the same number of rows as the left table.

Key Concepts
Inner Join
Keeps only matching rows
Unmatched rows are removed

Left Join
Keeps ALL rows from the left table
Missing matches from the right become NaN

Syntax
df1.merge(df2, on="column", how="left")

When Left Joins Are Useful
Left joins are extremely useful when:
one table is your “main” dataset
you do not want to lose rows
extra information from another table is optional
Examples:
customers + optional purchases
movies + optional taglines
students + optional scholarship info

Main Takeaway
A left join keeps every row from the left table, even when no matching data exists in the right table. Missing matches are filled with NaN, making left joins very useful when you want to preserve the full original dataset while adding extra information from another table.

t.cbtvxfsdf1pg.title: Other Types of Joins in pandas
t.cbtvxfsdf1pg.content:
Other Types of Joins in pandas
Previously, you learned about:
inner joins
left joins
This lesson introduces two more join types supported by pandas:
right join
outer join
These joins control which rows are kept after merging tables.

Right Join
A right join is basically the opposite of a left join.
It:
keeps all rows from the right table
only keeps matching rows from the left table
If no match exists in the left table, pandas fills the missing columns with NaN.

Visual Idea of a Right Join
Left Table

Example Using Movie Data
The lesson introduces another dataset called movie_to_genres.
A movie can belong to multiple genres, so this table stores movie IDs along with genre names.
The goal is to compare:
the movies table
the tv_genre subset
to check whether any movie information is missing.

Using Different Column Names
An important new concept appears here.
The matching columns do NOT always have the same name.
Example:
in movies → column is id
in tv_genre → column is movie_id
To handle this, pandas provides:
left_on
right_on

Right Join Syntax
movies.merge(
   tv_genre,
   how="right",
   left_on="id",
   right_on="movie_id"
)

Breaking Down the Code

Performs a right join.

left_on="id"
Uses the id column from the left table.

right_on="movie_id"
Uses the movie_id column from the right table.

Why This Is Useful
Sometimes datasets use different column names even though they represent the same thing.
Example:
customer_id
cust_id
id
left_on and right_on allow pandas to connect them correctly.

Outer Join
The last join type introduced is the outer join.
An outer join keeps:
ALL rows from the left table
AND ALL rows from the right table
Even if no matches exist.
Missing matches become NaN.

Outer Join Example
The lesson filters movie genres into two tiny tables:
Family movies
Comedy movies
Then merges them using an outer join.
family.merge(
   comedy,
   on="movie_id",
   how="outer",
   suffixes=("_fam", "_com")
)

New Concept: suffixes
If both tables contain columns with the same names, pandas automatically adds suffixes.
You can customize them using:
suffixes=("_fam", "_com")
This makes it easier to know which column came from which table.

Key Differences Between Join Types
Join Type
Keeps

Important Concepts

suffixes

Main Takeaway
Right joins and outer joins give you more control over which rows are preserved during merges. A right join keeps all rows from the right table, while an outer join keeps everything from both tables. pandas also allows merging on columns with different names using left_on and right_on, making joins much more flexible in real-world datasets.

t.3ciu9p3rjw6a.title: Merging a Table to Itself (Self Join)
t.3ciu9p3rjw6a.content:
Merging a Table to Itself (Self Join)
A self join happens when you merge a table with itself. This sounds strange at first, but it’s very useful when rows inside the same table are related to other rows in that same table.
The example in the lesson uses movie sequels.
Imagine a table like this:
id
title
sequel
862
Toy Story
863
863
Toy Story 2
10193
10193
Toy Story 3
NaN
The sequel column stores the ID of another movie inside the same table.
Toy Story (862) → sequel is movie 863
Toy Story 2 (863) → sequel is movie 10193
The problem is: the sequel’s title is not directly stored in the row — only its ID is.
So we merge the table with itself to connect:
original movie
sequel movie
into one row.

Basic Self Join
sequels.merge(
   sequels,
   left_on="sequel",
   right_on="id",
   suffixes=("_org", "_seq")
)

What Each Part Means
sequels.merge(sequels, ...)
You are merging the table with another copy of itself.
Think of it like:
left table  = original movies
right table = sequel movies
Even though they are the same DataFrame.

left_on="sequel"
Use the sequel column from the left table.
Example:
title
sequel
Toy Story
863

right_on="id"
Match it to the id column in the right table.
Example:
id
title
863
Toy Story 2
Since:
863 == 863
they get connected.

Result
title_org
title_seq
Toy Story
Toy Story 2
Toy Story 2
Toy Story 3
Now each movie is linked to its sequel.

Why suffixes is Needed
Both tables have columns like:
id
title
Without suffixes, pandas wouldn’t know which is which.
So:
suffixes=("_org", "_seq")
renames them internally to:
title_org
title_seq
meaning:
original movie
sequel movie

Inner Join vs Left Join
By default, merge uses an inner join.
That means:
only rows with matches are returned.
So movies without sequels disappear.
Example:
title
sequel
Titanic
NaN
Titanic gets removed because it has no matching sequel.

Using a Left Join
sequels.merge(
   sequels,
   left_on="sequel",
   right_on="id",
   how="left",
   suffixes=("_org", "_seq")
)
Now ALL original movies stay.
Movies without sequels will have:
NaN
for sequel columns.

Real-World Uses of Self Joins
Self joins are common in hierarchical or connected data.
Employee ↔ Manager
employee_id
manager_id
1
5
You can merge employees with employees again to get manager names.

Social Networks
user
friend_id
Alice
3
Merge users with users again to get friend information.

Logistics / Routes
city
next_city
Manila
Batangas
Self joins can connect travel paths.

Big Picture
A self join is basically:
“Use one row to look up another row in the same table.”
You are treating one DataFrame as if it were two related tables.

t.j5ws1afdf6mx.title: Merging on indexes
t.j5ws1afdf6mx.content:
Merging on Indexes
So far, merges used columns like:
movies.merge(taglines, on="id")
But pandas can also merge using the index of a DataFrame.
This is useful because indexes often contain unique IDs.

What is an Index Again?
Normally a DataFrame looks like this:
index
id
title
0
101
Avatar
1
102
Titanic
The leftmost numbers (0,1,2) are the default index.
But sometimes we make another column the index:
movies = movies.set_index("id")
Now:
id (index)
title
101
Avatar
102
Titanic
The id column became the index.

Why Merge on an Index?
Indexes are often:
unique
optimized for lookup
used as identifiers
So merging on indexes is clean and efficient.

Simple Index Merge
If both tables use the same index name:
movies.merge(taglines, on="id", how="left")
Even though id is now an index, pandas automatically understands it.

Big Picture
This works because:
on="id"
can refer to:
a column OR
an index name
pandas detects it automatically.

MultiIndex Merge
A MultiIndex means multiple index levels.
Example:
movie_id
cast_id
actor
1
10
Samuel Jackson
If both movie_id and cast_id are indexes:
samuel.merge(cast, on=["movie_id", "cast_id"])
This works exactly like merging on multiple columns.
Both values must match.

When Index Names are Different
Sometimes the indexes have different names.
Example:
Left table index:
id
Right table index:
movie_id
Then you use:
movies.merge(
   movie_to_genres,
   left_on="id",
   right_on="movie_id",
   left_index=True,
   right_index=True
)

Important Part
When using:
left_on
right_on
with indexes, you MUST specify:
left_index=True
right_index=True
This tells pandas:
“The keys are indexes, not regular columns.”

Quick Rule
Same index names
Use:
on="id"

Different index names
Use:
left_on=
right_on=
left_index=True
right_index=True

Conceptual Understanding
Think of indexes as:
hidden columns used to identify rows.
Normally merges use visible columns.
Index merges use those hidden identifiers instead.

Comparing Column Merge vs Index Merge
Column Merge
movies.merge(taglines, on="id")
Uses normal columns.

Index Merge
movies.set_index("id")
taglines.set_index("id")

movies.merge(taglines, on="id")
Uses indexes instead.

Important Insight
Indexes are mostly about:
faster lookup
cleaner subsetting
structured data relationships
And pandas lets merges work with them almost the same way as columns.
That’s why merging on indexes feels very similar to normal merging.

t.fa9ahp97u2ey.title: Filtering Joins
t.fa9ahp97u2ey.content:
Filtering Joins
Up to this point, the joins you learned were mostly mutating joins.
A mutating join:
combines columns from two tables.
Example:
movies.merge(taglines)
This adds new columns from another table.

Filtering Joins
Filtering joins are different.
Instead of adding columns, they:
filter rows based on whether matches exist in another table.
There are two main filtering joins:
Semi Join
Anti Join
pandas doesn’t have built-in methods named:
semi_join()
anti_join()
So we recreate them manually using:
merge()
isin()
filtering

Semi Join
A semi join returns:
rows from the LEFT table that HAVE matches in the RIGHT table.
Important:
only columns from the left table are returned
duplicates are not added
it behaves like a filter

Example
Suppose:
genres table
gid
genre
1
Rock
2
Jazz
3
Pop

top_tracks table
track
gid
Song A
1
Song B
3
We want:
genres that appear in top tracks.
Result:
gid
genre
1
Rock
3
Pop
Jazz is removed because it doesn’t appear.

Semi Join Process
Step 1 — Inner Merge
genres_tracks = genres.merge(top_tracks, on="gid")
This keeps only matching gids.

Step 2 — Use isin()
genres["gid"].isin(genres_tracks["gid"])
This checks:
“Does this gid exist in the merged table?”
Result:
True
False
True

Step 3 — Filter
top_genres = genres[genres["gid"].isin(genres_tracks["gid"])]
Now only matching genres remain.

Big Picture of Semi Join
Think of it as:
“Keep rows from the left table IF they exist in the right table.”
You are not interested in adding columns.
You only care whether a match exists.

Anti Join
An anti join is the opposite.
It returns:
rows from the LEFT table that DO NOT have matches in the RIGHT table.

Example
Using the same data:
genres
gid
genre
1
Rock
2
Jazz
3
Pop

top_tracks
track
gid
Song A
1
Song B
3
Result of anti join:
gid
genre
2
Jazz
Because Jazz never appeared in top tracks.

Anti Join Process
Step 1 — Left Merge with Indicator
genres_tracks = genres.merge(
   top_tracks,
   on="gid",
   how="left",
   indicator=True
)
The important part:
indicator=True
adds a special column:
_merge

_merge Values
The _merge column tells where the row came from.
Possible values:
value
meaning
both
exists in both tables
left_only
exists only in left
right_only
exists only in right

Step 2 — Get Unmatched Rows
gid_list = genres_tracks.loc[
   genres_tracks["_merge"] == "left_only",
   "gid"
]
This extracts gids that were NOT matched.

Step 3 — Filter Original Table
genres[genres["gid"].isin(gid_list)]
Now you get only genres absent from top_tracks.

Big Picture
Semi Join
KEEP matching rows

Anti Join
KEEP non-matching rows

Mental Model
Imagine two circles.
Inner Join
Returns the overlap AND combines columns.

Semi Join
Returns only the left-side rows that overlap.

Anti Join
Returns only the left-side rows outside the overlap.

Quick Comparison
Join Type
Purpose
Inner Join
combine matching rows
Left Join
keep all left rows
Semi Join
keep left rows WITH matches
Anti Join
keep left rows WITHOUT matches

Important Insight
Filtering joins are mostly used for:
existence checks
removing unmatched data
validating datasets
finding missing relationships
They are very common in data cleaning and analytics.
